why.correct: SHM needs a restoring force proportional to the displacement from equilibrium and opposite to it: F = −kx. Doubling x doubles F, and the sign is always opposite to x.
options: Right: this is the definition of the restoring force in SHM, F = −kx.
A zero force at equilibrium is true of any oscillation; it does not show the force grows in proportion to the displacement.

True of the data, but it says nothing about proportion or about the left side: a force that pointed left everywhere would never pull the glider back from the left. SHM needs F proportional to x and opposite to it.
Symmetry alone allows forces that are not proportional to x (for example a force that grows as x²).

why.correct: From any row, k = |F|/|x| = 2.4 N / 0.10 m = 24 N/m. Every row gives the same value, which is what makes the force proportional to x.
F = −kx = −(24 N/m)(0.080 m) = −1.92 N. a = F/m = −1.92 N / 0.40 kg = −4.8 m/s², toward equilibrium.
At x = 0 the spring is relaxed, so the spring force is zero; gravity and the normal force cancel on the level track. Zero net force means zero acceleration at that instant, not zero velocity.
options: Right: x = 0 is the equilibrium position, where the net force is zero.
This is the "a force is needed to keep it moving" idea. The glider keeps moving at x = 0 with no net force at that instant.
The force points left only once the glider is to the right of x = 0 and the spring is stretched.
This mixes up force with speed. The force depends on the displacement, which is zero here.

why.correct: At Y the string pulls straight up and Earth pulls straight down, so no force acts along the arc. That is the equilibrium position: the bob would stay there if placed at rest.
options: Right: at the equilibrium position the restoring force along the path is zero.
Being at rest for an instant does not make a point the equilibrium position. At X a restoring force pulls the bob back toward Y.
At Z the restoring force is largest, which is the opposite of equilibrium.
Y is the right point, but speed does not define equilibrium; the zero restoring force does.

why.correct: Amplitude is the largest displacement from equilibrium, measured from Y. The bob reaches 8° on each side.
options: Right: from Y to X (or to Z) is 8°.
This is the angle from one extreme to the other, which is twice the amplitude.
This halves the amplitude; the bob reaches the full 8° on each side.
The amplitude is not the displacement at equilibrium; it is the largest displacement.

why.correct: Along the arc, gravity has a part of size mg sin θ pointing back toward Y. For small angles sin θ ≈ θ (in radians), so the restoring force is close to mgθ = (mg/ℓ)s, proportional to the displacement s along the arc.
options: Right: a restoring force proportional to the displacement is what SHM needs.
The string force is not constant (it is largest at Y) and it points along the string, not along the path, so it is not the restoring force.
A constant downward force alone does not give a force proportional to the displacement along the arc.
Returning to the start shows periodic motion, not simple harmonic motion.

why.correct: 60° is 1.05 rad but sin 60° = 0.87, so the restoring force (mg sin θ) is 17% smaller than a force proportional to θ would be. The bob still swings back and forth, but the motion is no longer a close match to SHM.
options: Right: the small-angle approximation sin θ ≈ θ breaks down at large angles.
Oscillating about Y makes the motion periodic; SHM also needs the restoring force to be proportional to the displacement.
Without friction the bob repeats the same swing, so the motion is still periodic.
A larger force is not the test; the force must stay proportional to the displacement, and at 60° it falls short.

why.correct: SHM needs F = −kx: proportional to x and opposite to it. Here k = 6.0 N/m.
options: Right: proportional to the displacement and opposite to it.
This force points away from x = 0, so it pushes the object farther away; there is no oscillation.
This force is proportional to x², not x, and it points in −x on both sides, so it does not restore from the left.
A constant force does not depend on position at all, so it cannot pull back from both sides.

why.correct: Between bounces the only force is the ball's weight, mg downward, which does not change with height. SHM needs a restoring force that grows in proportion to the displacement from equilibrium.
options: Right: a constant force is not a restoring force proportional to displacement.
A pendulum is SHM with no spring; what matters is the form of the restoring force.
The stem says the ball rises to the same height each time, so the motion does repeat.
The ball is slowest at the top, not fastest.

why.correct: Equilibrium is halfway between the turning points, at 0.25 m. The amplitude is the largest displacement from there: 0.38 m − 0.25 m = 0.13 m.

At equilibrium the net force is zero: kΔx = mg, so Δx = mg/k = (0.50 kg)(9.8 m/s²)/(40 N/m) = 0.1225 m ≈ 0.12 m. For a hanging spring the equilibrium position is this stretched point, not the relaxed length.
Below equilibrium the spring is stretched more than at equilibrium, so its upward pull is larger than the weight. The net force points up, toward equilibrium, as a restoring force should.
options: Right: the spring force exceeds the weight below equilibrium.
The weight is there, but the spring's upward pull is larger at the lowest point.
At rest for an instant does not mean zero net force; this is where the net force is largest.
The net force does not follow the motion; it follows the displacement, pointing back toward equilibrium.

why.correct: The net force is −kx, so its size is largest where |x| is largest, at the turning points. By Newton's second law the acceleration is largest there too, even though the speed is zero.
options: Right: largest displacement, largest restoring force, largest acceleration.
At x = 0 the net force is zero, so the acceleration is zero; this is where the speed is greatest.
The force at ±A/2 is half its value at ±A.
A constant acceleration would need a constant force; the spring force changes with x.

why.correct: The restoring force is proportional to the displacement, F = −kx; the spring constant belongs to the spring.

variables.name: Size of the spring force at the moment of release
variables.why: F = kx and x doubled, so the force at release doubles.

variables.name: Size of the acceleration at the moment of release
variables.why: a = F/m: twice the force on the same mass gives twice the acceleration.

variables.name: Spring constant
variables.why: k is a property of the spring; pulling it farther does not change it.

why.correct: F = −kx: at the same x, doubling k doubles the force.
options: Right: F is proportional to k at a fixed displacement.
A stiffer spring pulls harder, not more gently.
F depends on k to the first power, not k².
The force depends on k as well as x.

why.correct: T = (time for 10 oscillations)/10 = 7.05 s / 10 = 0.705 s. Timing many oscillations and dividing shrinks the effect of your reaction time.
The 10-oscillation time goes from 7.05 s to 14.1 s, a factor of 2. T ∝ √m, and √4 = 2.
options: Right: the data and the equation both give a factor of 2.
The data show a factor of 2, not 4; and T depends on √m, not m.
The equation predicts a factor of √4 = 2, so the data agree with it.
A heavier block has more inertia, so it takes longer; the period grows.

why.correct: T = 14.1 s / 10 = 1.41 s. Square T = 2π√(m/k): T² = 4π²m/k, so k = 4π²m/T² = 4π²(0.80 kg)/(1.41 s)² = 15.9 N/m ≈ 16 N/m.
Squaring T = 2π√(m/k) gives T² = (4π²/k)·m, the form y = (slope)·x with y = T² and x = m. So k = 4π²/slope.
options: Right: T² is proportional to m, with slope 4π²/k.
T against m is a curve (T ∝ √m), so it has no single slope.
T against √m is a straight line, but its slope is 2π/√k, not k/2π.
The variables are right but the slope is upside down: T² = (4π²/k)m.

why.correct: T = 2π√(ℓ/g): the period depends on the length and g, not on the bob's mass or the (small) release angle. Pendulums 1 and 2 have the same length, 0.50 m.
options: Right: same length, so same period, despite different masses and angles.
These have the same mass and angle but different lengths, and length is what sets the period.
These have different lengths (0.50 m and 1.00 m).
These have different lengths (2.00 m and 1.00 m).

why.correct: T ∝ √ℓ. Pendulum 3 is 4 times as long (2.00 m vs 0.50 m), so its period is √4 = 2 times as long.
options: Right: four times the length gives twice the period.
This treats T as proportional to ℓ; it is proportional to √ℓ.
A longer pendulum swings more slowly, so its period is longer.
The bobs and angles match, but the lengths differ, and length sets the period.

why.correct: T ∝ 1/√g. With g one sixth as large, T is √6 ≈ 2.4 times as long. A weaker gravitational field gives a weaker restoring force.
options: Right: T = 2π√(ℓ/g), so T grows by √6.
The period depends on √g, not on g, so the factor is √6, not 6.
Smaller g means a weaker restoring force and slower swings: T grows.
g appears in the pendulum's period, so changing g changes T.

why.correct: f = number of cycles / time = 12 / 30.0 s = 0.40 Hz. The period is T = 1/f = 2.5 s.
Square T = 2π√(ℓ/g): T² = 4π²ℓ/g, so ℓ = gT²/(4π²) = (9.8 m/s²)(2.0 s)²/(4π²) = 0.99 m.
The period of a block on a spring depends on m and k: T = 2π√(m/k).

variables.name: The block is replaced by one with twice the mass
variables.why: T = 2π√(m/k): more mass, more inertia, longer period (by √2).

variables.name: The block is pulled twice as far before release
variables.why: A does not appear in T = 2π√(m/k): a larger amplitude means more distance but also more force and more speed.

variables.name: The spring is replaced by a stiffer one
variables.why: Larger k means a larger restoring force at each x, so the block turns around sooner.

why.correct: A pendulum's period depends on its length and on g, not on the bob's mass.

variables.name: The bob is replaced by one with twice the mass
variables.why: A heavier bob has a larger weight but also more inertia; m cancels and T = 2π√(ℓ/g) has no m.

variables.name: The string is made four times as long
The pendulum is taken to a planet with a stronger gravitational field
variables.why: Larger g gives a larger restoring force, so T = 2π√(ℓ/g) is shorter.

why.correct: For a pendulum, the restoring force comes from the bob's weight, which is proportional to its mass. Twice the mass gives twice the restoring force on twice the inertia, so the acceleration and the period do not change. Using the spring formula for a pendulum is a classic exam error.
options: Right: wrong formula for the system; the pendulum's period has no mass.
More inertia is matched by more weight pulling it back, so the two effects cancel.
An ideal string does not stretch, and the spring formula still does not apply.
The larger weight is canceled by the larger inertia; the period is unchanged.

why.correct: T = 2π√(m/k) contains neither g nor the stretch. Hanging the block moves the equilibrium position down, but about that new equilibrium the net restoring force is still −kx.
options: Right: same m and same k give the same period.
Gravity shifts where equilibrium is, not how fast the block oscillates about it.
Gravity is constant, so it cancels at the new equilibrium; it does not add to the restoring force.
Horizontally the spring alone is the restoring force, with the same k.

why.correct: T ∝ √m, so to double T you need √(new m / m) = 2, which gives 4m.
options: Right: four times the mass doubles the period.
Twice the mass gives √2 ≈ 1.41 times the period.
This multiplies the period by only about 1.19.
A smaller mass shortens the period.

why.correct: The cart is at +0.15 m at t = 0 and next at t = 0.80 s, so T = 0.80 s. Half a period (0.40 s) only takes it to the other side.
Speed is the steepness of the position-time graph. The graph is steepest where it crosses x = 0, at t = 0.20 s (and 0.60 s, 1.00 s...). The cart passes equilibrium at top speed.
options: Right: the slope is steepest where x = 0.
At 0.40 s the cart is at −0.15 m, a turning point: the slope is zero and the cart is momentarily at rest.
At 0.80 s the cart is back at +0.15 m, a turning point with zero speed.
At 0.30 s the cart is between equilibrium and a turning point; it is still moving, but slower than at 0.20 s.

why.correct: At 0.50 s the cart is below zero (x < 0) and the graph is rising, so v is +. The acceleration always points toward equilibrium, opposite to x; x is negative, so a is +.
options: Right: x < 0 and rising, so v > 0 and a = −(k/m)x > 0.
The graph is rising at 0.50 s (it left −0.15 m at 0.40 s), so the velocity is positive.
Acceleration is opposite to the displacement; with x negative, a is positive.
Both signs are off: the graph is rising at 0.50 s (v > 0), and with x below zero the acceleration points toward equilibrium (a > 0).

why.correct: Releasing from 0.075 m makes the amplitude 0.075 m, half of 0.15 m. The period T = 2π√(m/k) does not depend on the amplitude, so the peaks stay 0.80 s apart.
options: Right: smaller amplitude, same period.
A smaller amplitude does not shorten the period: less distance, but proportionally less force and speed.
The release point sets the amplitude, so the peaks must be lower.
The period depends on m and k only; amplitude does not lengthen it.

why.correct: Compare with x = A sin(2πft): f = 2.5 Hz, so T = 1/f = 0.40 s.
x = (0.040 m) sin(2π × 2.5 × 0.050) = (0.040 m) sin(0.785 rad) = (0.040 m)(0.707) = 0.028 m. That is one eighth of a period after it left equilibrium.
sin 0 = 0, so x = 0 at t = 0. Just after, sin is positive and growing, so the block moves in +x. At equilibrium its speed is at its largest.
options: Right: a sine graph starts at zero and rises.
That is how a cosine graph starts; this equation uses sine.
At equilibrium the block moves fastest; it is at rest only at the turning points.
sin 0 = 0, so the block is at x = 0, not at a turning point.

why.correct: 0.10 s is a quarter of the 0.40 s period: sin(2π × 2.5 × 0.10) = sin(π/2) = 1, so x = +0.040 m, a turning point. There v = 0, and the acceleration is largest and points toward equilibrium (−x).
options: Right: a quarter period after leaving equilibrium, the block is at +A.
x = 0 happens at t = 0 and 0.20 s, not at a quarter period.
At the turning point the block is momentarily at rest, not moving fastest.
The block reaches −0.040 m at three quarters of a period, t = 0.30 s.

why.correct: The period T = 2π√(m/k) is the same for both: block 2 travels twice as far but feels twice the force at each matching point, so it moves twice as fast. The two effects cancel.
options: Right: the period does not depend on the amplitude.
Block 1 does travel less distance, but it also moves more slowly; the times match.
Block 2 does feel a larger force, but it also has farther to go; the times match.
Less acceleration slows block 1 down, which works against it, not for it; the times still match.

why.correct: Moving from +A/2 toward x = 0 means moving in −x, so v is −. The acceleration points toward equilibrium, opposite to x; x is +, so a is −. Velocity and acceleration in the same direction means the object is speeding up, as it should on its way to equilibrium.
options: Right: v and a both point toward x = 0, so the object speeds up.
The acceleration is opposite to the displacement, not to the velocity. With x positive, a is negative.
Moving from +A/2 toward x = 0 is moving in the − direction, so v is negative.
The acceleration is zero only at x = 0. At x = +A/2 the restoring force is −kA/2, half its largest value.

why.correct: Set (0.12 m) cos(πt) = 0.060 m: cos(πt) = 0.5, so πt = π/3 and t = 1/3 s ≈ 0.33 s. The period is 2.0 s, so the cart covers the first half of its distance to equilibrium in one sixth of a period: it starts slowly.
At t = 0 the block must be at +A: cos 0 = 1 gives x = A. Both sine and cosine describe SHM; the starting point decides which one fits.
options: Right: cosine starts at its largest value.
This starts at x = 0, which fits a block that starts at equilibrium.
This starts at x = −A, the other turning point.
This oscillates between 0 and 2A, so its center is not the equilibrium position.

why.correct: Amplitude scales the size of x, v and a, but the timing (period) is set by m and k alone.

variables.name: Largest speed
variables.why: The block covers twice the distance in the same time, so its top speed doubles.

variables.name: Largest acceleration
variables.why: The largest force is kA, so it doubles with A, and a = F/m doubles too.

why.correct: v = 0 means a turning point. Before that instant v was +, so the object was moving toward +x and has just reached the + end, x = +A.
options: Right: moving + and stopping means it has reached +A.
At −A the velocity changes from − to +, the opposite crossing.
At equilibrium the speed is largest, so v is not zero there.
At equilibrium v has its largest size, not zero.

why.correct: v_max = 2πA/T = 2π(0.050 m)/(0.50 s) = 0.63 m/s. The average speed is 4A/T = 0.40 m/s; the top speed is higher because the mass slows near the ends.
At release the glider is at rest, so all the energy is in the spring: E = ½kA² = ½(50 N/m)(0.12 m)² = 0.36 J. With no friction this total stays the same throughout.
At x = 0 the spring has no energy, so K = E = 0.36 J. ½mv² = 0.36 J gives v = √(2 × 0.36 J / 0.50 kg) = √1.44 m/s = 1.2 m/s.
U_s = ½(50 N/m)(0.060 m)² = 0.090 J. K = E − U_s = 0.36 J − 0.09 J = 0.27 J: three quarters of the energy is kinetic at half the amplitude.

With no friction, the only force doing work on the glider is the spring force, which is internal to the glider-spring system and conservative. So the system's mechanical energy is constant, and at x = 0 all of it is kinetic energy.
options: Right: energy conservation with its condition (no nonconservative work).
Zero force at that instant does not explain why the speed is the same on every pass; the energy argument does.
The spring (attached to a wall) exerts an external force on the glider, and the glider's momentum keeps changing direction.
The period is unrelated; the speed at x = 0 depends on the energy, ½kA².

why.correct: Every row adds to 0.36 J, the constant total. K = 0.36 J − 0.16 J = 0.20 J.
At equilibrium the spring is at its relaxed length, so U_s = 0 and all the energy is kinetic. That is moment 3.
options: Right: U_s = 0 means x = 0.
At moment 1 K = 0: the block is at a turning point.
At moment 2 the spring still holds 0.09 J, so the block is displaced.
At moment 4 the spring holds 0.16 J.

why.correct: U_s = ½kx² and the total is ½kA². At moment 2, U_s/E = 0.09/0.36 = 1/4, so x²/A² = 1/4 and x = A/2.
options: Right: a quarter of the energy in the spring means half the amplitude.
This treats U_s as proportional to x; it goes as x².
This uses the kinetic share (3/4) as if it gave the position.
A/√2 is where the energy splits half and half.

why.correct: E = ½kA². Doubling A multiplies E by 2² = 4: 4 × 0.36 J = 1.44 J.
options: Right: total energy goes as the amplitude squared.
This doubles E; it should be multiplied by 4 because E depends on A².
The total energy depends on the amplitude; it is not fixed by the spring.
A larger amplitude stores more energy, not less.

why.correct: Total energy depends on k and A; the period depends on m and k.

variables.name: Total mechanical energy
variables.why: E = ½kA²: four times k at the same A gives four times the energy.

variables.name: Period
variables.why: T = 2π√(m/k): four times k halves the period.

why.correct: The bob drops in height, so U_g decreases; with no air resistance and a string that does no work (it pulls at right angles to the motion), the total is constant, so K rises by exactly that amount.
options: Right: a constant total means the gain in K equals the loss in U_g.
With no energy coming in from outside the system, both cannot increase.
Speeding up is energy changing form, not energy being used up.
U_g = mgy depends on height, and the bob gets lower.

why.correct: With no nonconservative work done, the mechanical energy K + U stays constant; only how it is split changes.
options: Right: E = K + U is constant.
K goes from zero at the ends to its largest value at equilibrium.
U is largest at the ends and smallest at equilibrium.
The speed changes from zero to its top value and back.

why.correct: Energy at x = 0 (all kinetic) equals energy at x = A (all spring): ½mv² = ½kA², so A = v√(m/k) = (0.60 m/s)√(0.20 kg / 80 N/m) = (0.60 m/s)(0.050 s) = 0.030 m.
Equal shares means U_s = E/2: ½kx² = ½(½kA²), so x² = A²/2 and x = ±A/√2 ≈ ±0.71A.
options: Right: half the energy in the spring means x² = A²/2.
At A/2 the spring holds only a quarter of the energy, because U_s goes as x².
At x = 0 all the energy is kinetic.
At the turning points all the energy is in the spring.

why.correct: At x = ±A the kinetic energy is zero, but the spring is stretched or compressed the most, so U_s = ½kA², the whole total.
options: Right: zero kinetic energy is not zero total energy.
At the turning points the mass is momentarily at rest, so K is zero.
At equilibrium U_s = 0, but the mass is moving fastest, so K holds all the energy.
The total mechanical energy is constant with no friction; it never drops to zero.

why.correct: For the bob-Earth system with negligible air resistance: mgΔy = ½mv², so v = √(2gΔy) = √(2 × 9.8 m/s² × 0.080 m) = 1.25 m/s ≈ 1.3 m/s. The mass cancels.
The largest K equals the total E = ½kA², which goes as A². Tripling A gives 3² = 9 times the energy.
options: Right: energy goes as amplitude squared.
This treats the energy as proportional to A, not A².
The energy grows faster than A, not more slowly.
More amplitude stores more energy in the spring at release.
